questions.prompt: Which of these is copied by value when you assign it to another variable?
questions.explanation: Primitives like numbers are copied. Arrays, objects and functions are objects, so only the reference is copied.

questions.prompt: `const a = [1, 2]; const b = a; b.push(3);` What is `a` now?
questions.explanation: `a` and `b` point to the same array. `const` only stops you from reassigning `a`; it does not stop changes to the array.

questions.prompt: What does `{} === {}` return?
questions.explanation: Each `{}` creates a new object. `===` on objects checks whether both sides are the same object.

questions.prompt: Why does React not re-render after `state.items.push(x); setState(state);`?
options: The state is still the same object, so React sees no change
questions.correct_answer: The state is still the same object, so React sees no change
questions.explanation: React compares the old and new state by reference. Create a new object, for example `{ ...state, items: [...state.items, x] }`.

questions.prompt: With `const a = { n: 1 }; const b = { n: 1 };`, which check is true?
questions.explanation: The numbers inside are equal primitives. The objects themselves are two different objects, so every reference check is false.

questions.prompt: `const user = { name: "Ann" }; const copy = { ...user }; copy.name = "Bob";` What is `user.name`?
questions.explanation: Spread creates a new object. Changing a top-level property of the copy does not touch the original.

questions.prompt: `function reset(obj) { obj = {}; } const o = { n: 1 }; reset(o);` What is `o.n` after the call?
questions.explanation: Reassigning the parameter only points the local variable at a new object. The caller's `o` still points to the old one.

questions.prompt: `const list = [{ id: 1 }]; const copy = [...list]; copy[0].id = 2;` What is `list[0].id`?
questions.explanation: The new array still holds the same object inside. Spread copies only the top level.

questions.prompt: Why is `useEffect(() => { ... }, [{ id: 1 }])` a problem?
options: A new object is created on each render, so the dependency never matches and the effect runs every time
Objects are not allowed as dependencies
questions.correct_answer: A new object is created on each render, so the dependency never matches and the effect runs every time
questions.explanation: React compares dependencies by reference. Use primitive values like `id`, or keep the object stable with `useMemo`.
Strings are primitives, so `b` gets its own copy. Changing `b` leaves `a` alone.
`a` and `b` are the same object, so the change shows through both, and `===` is true.
`push` changes the caller's array. Reassigning `list` afterwards only changes the local variable, which is what gets returned.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between copying by value and copying by reference?
key_points: Primitives are copied by value, so the copy is independent
Objects, arrays and functions are copied by reference, so both variables point to the same object
A change made through one variable shows through the other
questions.correct_answer: Primitives like numbers and strings are copied by value: the new variable gets its own copy, and changing it does not affect the original. Objects, arrays and functions are copied by reference: both variables point to the same object in memory. So if you change a property through one variable, the other sees the change too.

questions.prompt: Why does mutating state in React not cause a re-render?
key_points: React compares the old and new state by reference, using `Object.is`
Mutating keeps the same reference, so React sees no change
You should create a new object or array, for example with spread, `map` or `filter`
Mutation also breaks `memo`, `useMemo` and `useEffect` dependencies
questions.correct_answer: React decides whether state changed by checking if the new value is the same reference as the old one. If you mutate an object and pass it back, it is still the same object, so React thinks nothing changed and skips the render. The fix is to create a new object or array, with spread, `map` or `filter`. Mutation also confuses `memo` and effect dependencies, which compare by reference too.

questions.prompt: How does `===` compare objects, and how would you compare two objects by their content?
key_points: `===` compares references, so it is true only for the very same object
Two objects with the same content are still not equal with `===`
To compare content, write a deep equality function that compares keys and values recursively
`JSON.stringify` is a shortcut but fails on key order, `undefined`, functions and dates
questions.correct_answer: `===` on objects checks whether both sides are the same object, not whether they look the same, so `{ a: 1 } === { a: 1 }` is false. To compare content you need a deep equality check: make sure both have the same keys, then compare each value, going into nested objects recursively. Comparing `JSON.stringify` output is a quick trick, but it breaks when keys are in a different order and it drops `undefined` and functions.

questions.prompt: What does a shallow copy copy?
options: Only the top level; nested objects are still shared
Nothing; it is just a reference
questions.correct_answer: Only the top level; nested objects are still shared
questions.explanation: A shallow copy is a new outer object, but nested objects inside it are the same ones as in the original.

questions.prompt: Which of these makes a shallow copy of an object?
questions.explanation: Spread copies the top-level properties into a new object. Plain `obj` is the same reference.

questions.prompt: Which built-in function makes a deep copy?
questions.explanation: `structuredClone` copies every level. `Object.assign` and `Array.from` are shallow.

questions.prompt: `const a = { user: { name: "Ann" } }; const b = { ...a }; b.user.name = "Bob";` What is `a.user.name`?
questions.explanation: Spread is shallow, so `a.user` and `b.user` are the same object.

questions.prompt: What does `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` lose?
options: Functions and `undefined` values, and `Date` objects become strings
questions.correct_answer: Functions and `undefined` values, and `Date` objects become strings
questions.explanation: JSON has no functions, `undefined` or dates. It also fails on circular references.

questions.prompt: How is `Object.assign(target, source)` different from `{ ...source }`?
options: It copies into an existing target object and changes it; both are shallow
questions.correct_answer: It copies into an existing target object and changes it; both are shallow
questions.explanation: `Object.assign({}, source)` behaves like spread. With an existing target, that target is mutated.

questions.prompt: Which of these makes `structuredClone` throw?
options: An object with a function in it, such as a method
questions.correct_answer: An object with a function in it, such as a method
questions.explanation: `structuredClone` handles dates, maps, sets and circular references, but throws a `DataCloneError` on functions and DOM nodes.

questions.prompt: In a reducer, which is the correct way to update `state.user.address.city`?
questions.explanation: Every level along the path must be a new object. The other options either mutate or put `city` in the wrong place.

questions.prompt: Why can you write `state.user.name = x` in a Redux Toolkit reducer?
options: Immer records changes on a draft and builds a new immutable state for you
Redux Toolkit allows real mutation of the state
It deep clones the whole state on every action
It freezes the state so the change is ignored
questions.correct_answer: Immer records changes on a draft and builds a new immutable state for you
questions.explanation: The reducer receives a draft. Immer turns your changes into new objects only along the changed path.
Spread makes a new array, so pushing to `b` does not change `a`.
The copy is shallow, so `a.tags` and `b.tags` are the same array.
The JSON trick turns the date into a string and drops `undefined`. `structuredClone` keeps the `Date` and makes a new nested array.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
key_points: A shallow copy copies only the top level; nested objects are shared
A deep copy copies every level, so nothing is shared
Changing nested data in a shallow copy also changes the original
questions.correct_answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer object, but any nested objects or arrays inside it are still the same ones as in the original. A deep copy copies every level, so the copy shares nothing with the original. With a shallow copy, changing a nested value changes the original too, which is a common bug.

questions.prompt: How do spread, `Object.assign` and `structuredClone` differ?
key_points: Spread creates a new shallow copy
`Object.assign` copies properties into a target object, changing it; it is also shallow
`structuredClone` makes a deep copy and handles dates, maps, sets and circular references
`structuredClone` cannot copy functions
questions.correct_answer: Spread, `{ ...obj }`, makes a new object with the same top-level properties: a shallow copy. `Object.assign(target, obj)` copies properties into the target and changes it, also only one level deep. `structuredClone(obj)` makes a full deep copy and supports dates, maps, sets and circular references, but it throws on functions.

questions.prompt: How do you update nested state immutably in React or Redux?
key_points: Copy every level along the path you change, using spread
Leave the branches you did not change shared
Never mutate the existing state
Immer, used by Redux Toolkit, lets you write changes on a draft and builds the new state
Deep cloning the whole state is wasteful and breaks memoisation
questions.correct_answer: To change a nested value, you make a new object at every level along the path: a new state, a new `user`, a new `address`, each made with spread. Branches you did not touch stay shared, which is cheap and keeps memoisation working. You never mutate the old state. Redux Toolkit uses Immer, so you can write `state.user.address.city = x` on a draft and Immer creates the new objects. Deep cloning everything would work but creates new references everywhere and causes extra renders.

questions.prompt: `const { name } = { name: "Ann", age: 30 };` What is `name`?
questions.explanation: Object destructuring reads the property with the same name as the variable.

questions.prompt: `const [first, second] = [10, 20, 30];` What is `second`?
questions.explanation: Array destructuring works by position. Extra items are ignored.

questions.prompt: In `function sum(...nums) {}`, what is `nums`?
options: An array of all the arguments
questions.correct_answer: An array of all the arguments
questions.explanation: A rest parameter collects the arguments into a real array.

questions.prompt: `const { a = 5 } = { a: undefined };` What is `a`?
questions.explanation: A default value is used when the value is `undefined`.

questions.prompt: `const { a = 5 } = { a: null };` What is `a`?
questions.explanation: Defaults apply only to `undefined`. `null` is a real value, so it is kept.

questions.prompt: What does `const { name: userName } = user;` do?
questions.explanation: The part before the colon is the property, and the part after is the new variable name.

questions.prompt: `let a = 1, b = 2; [a, b] = [b, a];` What are `a` and `b` now?
questions.explanation: The right side builds the array `[2, 1]` first, then destructuring assigns it. This swaps two variables without a temporary one.

questions.prompt: What does `{ ...{ a: 1, b: 2 }, a: 3 }` give?
questions.explanation: Properties written later win. This is how you override one field in an update.

questions.prompt: What happens with `const { x: { y } } = { x: null };`?
questions.explanation: Nested destructuring reads `y` from `null`, which throws. A default like `{ x: { y } = {} }` does not help with `null`, only with `undefined`.
Each variable takes the property with its own name.
The rest parameter collects everything after `first`. With one argument it is an empty array.
Spread copies `size: undefined` over the default 2. Destructuring then uses its own default 1, because the value is `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What is destructuring?
key_points: A short way to unpack values from arrays or objects into variables
Arrays are unpacked by position, objects by property name
You can set default values and rename variables
questions.correct_answer: Destructuring is a short syntax for pulling values out of arrays and objects into variables. With arrays it works by position, as in `const [a, b] = list`. With objects it works by property name, as in `const { name } = user`. You can also give defaults, `{ size = 1 }`, and rename, `{ name: userName }`.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between spread and rest?
key_points: Both use the same `...` syntax
Spread expands an array or object into separate items, for example to copy or to pass arguments
Rest collects the remaining items into an array or object
Rest is used in parameters and destructuring and must come last
questions.correct_answer: Both use `...`, but they do opposite things. Spread takes an array or object and expands it, for example `[...list, item]`, `{ ...obj }` or `fn(...args)`. Rest collects what is left over into one array or object, as in `function f(...args)` or `const { a, ...others } = obj`. Rest must be the last item.

questions.prompt: How are destructuring, spread and rest used in React?
key_points: Props are destructured in the function parameters, like `function Card({ title })`
`useState` returns an array that is destructured, like `[count, setCount]`
Spread creates new state, like `{ ...state, x }` or `[...items, item]`
Rest passes the remaining props on, like `{ className, ...rest }` and then `{...rest}`
questions.correct_answer: Components destructure their props right in the parameters, like `function Card({ title, onClick })`. Hooks return arrays that you destructure, like `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`. Spread is how you make new state without mutating, `setUser({ ...user, name })` or `[...items, item]`. Rest lets a wrapper component pick a few props and pass the rest on with `{...rest}`.

questions.prompt: What is a prototype in JavaScript?
options: An object that another object inherits properties from
A draft version of a function
questions.correct_answer: An object that another object inherits properties from
questions.explanation: Each object has a hidden link to its prototype. Properties not found on the object are looked up there.

questions.prompt: Where does `[1, 2].map` come from?
questions.explanation: Arrays do not store `map` themselves. They find it on `Array.prototype` through the prototype chain.

questions.prompt: What is at the end of almost every prototype chain?
questions.explanation: That is why every object has methods like `hasOwnProperty` and `toString`.

questions.prompt: How does JavaScript look up `obj.x`?
options: It checks `obj`, then its prototype, then that prototype's prototype, until it finds `x` or reaches `null`
It searches every object in memory
It checks the global scope first
questions.correct_answer: It checks `obj`, then its prototype, then that prototype's prototype, until it finds `x` or reaches `null`
questions.explanation: If nothing in the chain has `x`, the result is `undefined`.

questions.prompt: `const parent = { hi: () => "hi" }; const child = Object.create(parent);` What does `child.hasOwnProperty("hi")` return?
questions.explanation: `child.hi` works, but it is found on the prototype. `hasOwnProperty` only checks the object itself.

questions.prompt: What does `Object.getPrototypeOf([])` return?
questions.explanation: An array's prototype is `Array.prototype`. `Array` is the constructor function, not the prototype.

questions.prompt: `const parent = { n: 1 }; const child = Object.create(parent); child.n = 2;` What is `parent.n`?
questions.explanation: Assigning creates an own property on `child` that hides the inherited one. The prototype is not changed.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `prototype` and `__proto__`?
options: `prototype` is a property of functions, used for objects made with `new`; `__proto__` is an object's link to its own prototype
questions.correct_answer: `prototype` is a property of functions, used for objects made with `new`; `__proto__` is an object's link to its own prototype
questions.explanation: `new User()` creates an object whose `__proto__` is `User.prototype`. Prefer `Object.getPrototypeOf` over `__proto__`.

questions.prompt: Why is adding methods to `Array.prototype` a bad idea?
options: Every array in the app and its libraries gets the method, which can clash with other code or future built-ins
questions.correct_answer: Every array in the app and its libraries gets the method, which can clash with other code or future built-ins
questions.explanation: This has happened before: a library's `Array.prototype.flatten` delayed the built-in `flat`. Write a helper function instead.
`eats` is found on the prototype, but `Object.keys` lists only the object's own properties, and it has none.
`hi` lives once on `User.prototype` and is shared by every user, so it is not an own property and both users get the same function.
`this.count++` reads 0 from the prototype, then writes the result as an own property on `a`. The prototype keeps 0.

questions.prompt: What is a prototype?
key_points: Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype
If a property is not on the object, JavaScript looks for it on the prototype
This is how arrays get `map` and `filter` from `Array.prototype`
questions.correct_answer: A prototype is an object that another object inherits from. Every object has a hidden link to its prototype. When you read a property the object does not have, JavaScript looks for it on the prototype. That is how every array can call `map` and `filter`: those methods live once on `Array.prototype`.

questions.prompt: How does property lookup work along the prototype chain?
key_points: JavaScript checks the object's own properties first
Then it checks the prototype, then the prototype's prototype, and so on
It stops at `null` and returns `undefined` if nothing was found
Writing a property creates an own property that hides the inherited one; it does not change the prototype
questions.correct_answer: When you read `obj.x`, JavaScript first checks whether `obj` has its own `x`. If not, it checks `obj`'s prototype, then that object's prototype, and so on. The chain ends at `Object.prototype`, whose prototype is `null`; if `x` was not found anywhere, the result is `undefined`. Writing `obj.x = 1` does not go up the chain: it creates an own property on `obj` that hides the inherited one.

questions.prompt: How do classes relate to prototypes?
key_points: Classes are mostly a nicer syntax over prototypes
Methods are stored once on `ClassName.prototype` and shared by every instance
`extends` links the child's prototype to the parent's prototype
Fields set in the constructor are own properties of each instance
questions.correct_answer: A class is mostly a clearer way to write prototype-based code. The class is a constructor function, and its methods are stored once on `ClassName.prototype`, where every instance finds them through the chain. `extends` links `Child.prototype` to `Parent.prototype`, so a child instance can find parent methods. Fields and values set in the constructor are stored on each instance as own properties.

questions.prompt: What does `new User()` return when the constructor does not return anything?
questions.explanation: `new` creates an object, runs the constructor with `this` set to it, and returns it.

questions.prompt: Inside a class, which method runs when you call `new`?
questions.explanation: The `constructor` method sets up each new instance.

questions.prompt: What does `class Admin extends User` do?
questions.explanation: `extends` links the prototypes, so `Admin` instances find `User` methods through the chain.

questions.prompt: In a child class constructor, what must you do before using `this`?
questions.explanation: The parent constructor creates the object. Using `this` before `super()` throws a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: What does `typeof class User {}` return?
questions.explanation: A class is a special kind of function underneath.

questions.prompt: Can you call a class without `new`, like `User()`?
options: Yes, it works the same as with `new`
Yes, it returns the class itself
questions.explanation: Unlike old constructor functions, classes must be called with `new`.

questions.prompt: Which list shows what `new User()` does, in order?
options: Create an empty object, link it to `User.prototype`, run `User` with `this` set to it, return it
Run `User`, then create an object, then link it to the prototype
Copy `User.prototype` into a new object, then run `User`
Create an object, run `User`, then link it to `Object.prototype`
questions.correct_answer: Create an empty object, link it to `User.prototype`, run `User` with `this` set to it, return it
questions.explanation: One exception: if the constructor returns an object, `new` returns that object instead.

questions.prompt: What does `static` mean on a class method?
options: The method belongs to the class itself, not to instances
questions.correct_answer: The method belongs to the class itself, not to instances
questions.explanation: You call it as `User.create()`, not `user.create()`. It is often used for factory helpers.

questions.prompt: What is `#count` in `class Counter { #count = 0; }`?
options: A private field that only code inside the class can read
questions.correct_answer: A private field that only code inside the class can read
questions.explanation: Reading `counter.#count` outside the class is a SyntaxError. This is real privacy, unlike the old `_count` naming habit.
The constructor stores `name` on the new object, and `bark` reads it through `this`.
`super.speak()` calls the parent's method. A `Cat` is also an `Animal`, because `Animal.prototype` is in its chain.
When a constructor returns an object, `new` returns that object and throws away the one it created.

questions.prompt: What does `new` do?
key_points: Creates a new empty object
Links the object's prototype to the constructor's `prototype`
Runs the constructor with `this` set to the new object
Returns the new object, unless the constructor returns another object
questions.correct_answer: `new` creates a new empty object and links it to the constructor's `prototype`, so it can use the shared methods. Then it runs the constructor with `this` set to that object, so the constructor can add properties. Finally it returns the object. The only exception is when the constructor returns its own object; then that one is returned instead.

questions.prompt: Are JavaScript classes just prototypes underneath?
key_points: Mostly yes: a class is a function, and its methods live on its prototype
`extends` links the prototypes of the two classes
Differences: classes must be called with `new`, and class code runs in strict mode
Classes are not usable before their line (temporal dead zone), and they support private fields
questions.correct_answer: Mostly, yes. A class is a constructor function, its methods are stored on `ClassName.prototype`, and `extends` links the prototype of the child to that of the parent. But classes are not only sugar: they throw if called without `new`, their code always runs in strict mode, and they cannot be used before their line. They also add features like private `#fields`.

questions.prompt: When would you use a class in a frontend or Node project?
key_points: Custom error classes that extend `Error` and carry extra information
Services or API clients that keep their own setup, like a base URL
Node frameworks such as NestJS are built around classes
Modern React uses functions and hooks; classes appear in older code and error boundaries
questions.correct_answer: Custom errors are a common case: `class NotFoundError extends Error` lets you add a status code and check the type with `instanceof`. A class also fits an API client or service that keeps its own setup, like a base URL and token. Node frameworks like NestJS use classes everywhere. In modern React you write function components with hooks; classes are mostly found in older code and in error boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which method changes the original array?
questions.explanation: `sort` sorts the array in place. `map`, `filter` and `slice` return a new array.

questions.prompt: What does `toSorted()` do?
options: Returns a sorted copy and leaves the original unchanged
questions.correct_answer: Returns a sorted copy and leaves the original unchanged
questions.explanation: `toSorted` is the non-mutating version of `sort`.

questions.prompt: Which method returns a new array?
questions.explanation: `concat` builds a new array. The other three change the original.

questions.prompt: `const a = [3, 1, 2]; const b = a.sort();` What is `a === b`?
options: `true`, because `sort` sorts in place and returns the same array
questions.correct_answer: `true`, because `sort` sorts in place and returns the same array
questions.explanation: `sort` changes `a` and returns `a` itself, not a copy.

questions.prompt: What does `push` return?
options: The new length of the array
questions.correct_answer: The new length of the array
questions.explanation: This is why `const list = arr.push(x)` is a common bug: `list` is a number.

questions.prompt: Which are the non-mutating versions of `reverse` and `splice`?
questions.explanation: Along with `toSorted` and `with`, they return new arrays and leave the original alone.

questions.prompt: What does `[1, 2, 3].with(1, 9)` return?
options: It changes the original to `[1, 9, 3]` and returns `undefined`
questions.explanation: `with(index, value)` returns a copy with one item replaced: the non-mutating version of `arr[1] = 9`.

questions.prompt: Why is `setItems(items.sort())` a bug in React?
options: `sort` changes the state array in place and returns the same array, so React may not re-render
questions.correct_answer: `sort` changes the state array in place and returns the same array, so React may not re-render
questions.explanation: React compares by reference. Use `setItems(items.toSorted())` or `[...items].sort()`.

questions.prompt: What does `["a", "b", "c"].splice(1, 1)` return?
questions.explanation: `splice` returns an array of what it removed, and changes the original to `["a", "c"]`.
`toSorted` returns a sorted copy, so `nums` keeps its order.
`reverse` changes `a` and returns the same array, so pushing to `b` also changes `a`.
`splice` changes `list` and returns the removed items. `toSpliced` and `with` return new arrays and leave their input alone.

questions.prompt: Name array methods that change the original array, and some that return a new array.
key_points: Mutating: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`, `fill`
New array: `map`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat`, `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `with`
The difference matters when the array is shared, for example React state
questions.correct_answer: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse` and `fill` change the array you call them on. `map`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat` and the newer `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with` return a new array and leave the original alone. It matters whenever other code holds the same array, like React state or a prop.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `sort` and `toSorted`?
key_points: `sort` sorts in place and returns the same array
`toSorted` returns a new sorted array and leaves the original unchanged
Both compare as strings by default unless you pass a compare function
In React, use `toSorted`, or copy the array first, to avoid mutating state
questions.correct_answer: `sort` rearranges the original array and returns that same array. `toSorted` returns a sorted copy and leaves the original as it was. Both compare items as strings unless you pass a compare function, so numbers need `(a, b) => a - b`. In React state, `toSorted` is the safe choice, because it gives React a new reference.

questions.prompt: How do you update an array in React state without mutating it?
key_points: Add with spread: `[...items, item]`
Remove with `filter`
Update one item with `map`, returning a new object for it
Sort or reverse with `toSorted` and `toReversed`, or copy first
Replace an item by index with `with`
questions.correct_answer: I always build a new array. To add, `[...items, item]`; to remove, `items.filter((i) => i.id !== id)`; to change one item, `items.map((i) => (i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i))`. To sort or reverse, I use `toSorted` and `toReversed` instead of `sort` and `reverse`, and `with` to replace by index. The new reference is what tells React to re-render.
